KOSPI Stages Dramatic Intraday Reversal, Closes Slightly Higher
Korea Markets · 
[수정] May 18, 2026
The index fell more than 4% at the open — triggering a sidecar halt — before recovering fully to close up 0.31%, as domestic buyers overwhelmed a massive foreign selloff.
KOSPI close
 7,516.04

 move ≥5% for 1 minute. Korea’s volatility circuit breaker.
Seoul opened sharply lower, weighed down by Friday’s Wall Street decline — driven by renewed inflation concerns and Middle East tensions — and continued foreign outflows that have persisted since May 7. 
[수정] A sidecar was triggered early in the session, suspending program trading as KOSPI 200 futures breached the ≥5% threshold.
The reversal came swiftly. Domestic retail and institutional investors bought heavily into the dip. Separately, a Seoul court issued an injunction blocking Samsung Electronics’ largest union from proceeding with a planned strike on May 21, easing what had been a significant near-term overhang for the index’s largest constituent.
Capital flows
Investor typeFlowForeign investors–₩3.65T (~$2.7B)Retail (domestic)+₩2.21T (~$1.6B)Institutional+₩1.39T (~$1.0B)
Foreign selling exceeded the combined domestic buying by roughly $100M, yet the index finished positive — a sign of concentrated retail demand in key large-caps rather than broad-based support.

Three things to watch
1. Samsung labor risk
 The court injunction is a temporary reprieve. If union negotiations stall, a strike threat could re-emerge. Samsung accounts for roughly 20% of KOSPI’s market cap — any sustained disruption would have outsized index impact.
2. USD/KRW at 1,500
 The won has been at or above the 1,500 level — a rate historically associated with crisis periods (1997 IMF bailout, 2008 GFC). Sustained weakness here adds FX risk for foreign investors holding Korean assets.
3. Foreign flow trend
 Today’s $2.7B in foreign selling is not a one-off. Outflows have been running continuously since May 7. Whether this is tactical positioning or a structural rotation away from Korean equities is the key question for the weeks ahead.

📖 Korea Market Glossary — Everything You Need to Read Seoul Inside
A living reference guide for international readers. Bookmark this post and refer back anytime.
🏛️ Market Structure
KOSPI
(Korea Composite Stock Price Index)
 Korea’s main benchmark index, equivalent to the S&P 500. Tracks all common stocks listed on the Korea Exchange (KRX). When Koreans say “the market,” they mean the KOSPI.
KOSDAQ
 Korea’s second exchange, focused on small- and mid-cap tech and biotech companies — similar in spirit to Nasdaq. More volatile than the KOSPI.
KOSPI 200
 A sub-index of the 200 largest and most liquid KOSPI stocks. Important because derivatives (futures, options) are based on this index — not the broader KOSPI. 
[수정] The sidecar is triggered by KOSPI 200 futures movements. The circuit breaker, however, is triggered by declines in the KOSPI index itself — not futures.
KRX
(Korea Exchange)
 Korea’s single, unified stock exchange where all equities, bonds, and derivatives trade. Unlike the US, which splits trading across NYSE, Nasdaq, and others, Korea has just one exchange. Run by a government-backed public corporation.
⚡ Circuit Breakers & Volatility Controls
Sidecar
(프로그램 매매 호가 효력 일시정지)
 A 5-minute suspension of 
program trading orders only
 — triggered when KOSPI 200 futures move ≥5% from the previous day’s close for 1 consecutive minute. Regular buy/sell orders from individuals continue during a sidecar. It can only be triggered once per session, and never in the final 40 minutes of trading.
vs. US Circuit Breaker:
 The US circuit breaker halts 
all
 trading market-wide (at –7%, –13%, –20%). Korea’s sidecar is narrower — it targets only algorithmic basket trades, acting as a speed bump rather than a full stop.
Circuit Breaker
(매매거래 중단)
 Korea’s full trading halt. Triggered when the KOSPI falls ≥8% from the prior close for 1 minute. All trading stops for 20 minutes. A second trigger at –15% halts trading again; a third at –20% closes the market for the day. Far rarer than the sidecar.
VI
(Volatility Interruption, 변동성 완화 장치)
 A stock-level pause (not market-wide) triggered when an individual stock’s price moves too fast within a short window. Trading in that single stock pauses for 2 minutes while an auction determines a fair price. Happens dozens of times daily across the market.
👥 Investor Types & Flow Data
One of Korea’s most distinctive features: the KRX publishes 
real-time net buying/selling data
 broken into three groups. This transparency is rare globally — most markets don’t disclose this in real time.
Foreign Investors
(외국인)
 Overseas institutions and funds. Historically hold ~30% of KOSPI market cap — far higher than the ~15% foreign ownership typical in US equities. Because of this, foreign flows have an outsized impact on the index. When foreigners sell heavily, the market feels it immediately.
Retail Investors
(개인 / 개미)
 Domestic individual investors. Called 
개미
 (ants) — small but numerous. Korean retail participation is among the highest in the world. During market drops, retail investors often “buy the dip” aggressively, acting as a market stabilizer.
Institutional Investors
(기관)
 Domestic institutions: pension funds (NPS — Korea’s giant national pension), insurance companies, mutual funds, and securities firms trading on their own account. NPS alone manages over $700B and is a major price-setter.
NPS
(National Pension Service, 국민연금)
 Korea’s national pension fund, one of the largest sovereign-linked funds in the world. Its buying and selling decisions can move the KOSPI meaningfully. When NPS is a buyer, the market pays attention.
💱 Currency
USD/KRW
 The US dollar to Korean won exchange rate. Quoted as the number of won per one dollar — so a higher number means a 
weaker
 won. For example, USD/KRW 1,500 means ₩1,500 buys $1.
Key historical levels:
~1,100–1,200
 — normal, stable range (2010s)
~1,500
 — historically associated with crisis (1997 IMF bailout, 2008 GFC)
~2,000
 — seen briefly during the 1997–98 Asian financial crisis
A weak won raises costs for Korean companies that import raw materials, but can help exporters like Samsung and Hyundai by making their products cheaper abroad.
🏢 Key Companies & Market Structure
Samsung Electronics
(005930.KS)
 The single largest company on the KOSPI, accounting for roughly 20% of the index’s total market cap. A global leader in memory chips (DRAM, NAND), smartphones, and display panels. When Samsung moves, the KOSPI moves.
SK Hynix
(000660.KS)
 The world’s second-largest memory chip maker (after Samsung). Heavily tied to the global AI and data center boom — its HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) chips are used in Nvidia’s AI GPUs.
Chaebol
(재벌)
 Korea’s large family-controlled conglomerates. Samsung, SK, Hyundai, LG, Lotte — these groups dominate the Korean economy. A single chaebol family typically controls dozens of affiliated companies through cross-shareholding. Understanding chaebol structure is key to understanding Korean equities.
The top 10 KOSPI stocks account for over 50% of the index — a much higher concentration than the S&P 500.
📊 Data & Terminology
Market Cap Weighting
 The KOSPI is a market-cap weighted index, like the S&P 500. Larger companies move the index more. Samsung’s ~20% weight means a 5% move in Samsung Electronics shifts the KOSPI by roughly 1% all by itself.
Tick Size
 The minimum price movement for a stock. In Korea, tick sizes vary by price range — unlike the uniform $0.01 tick in the US.
T+2 Settlement
 Korean equities settle 2 business days after the trade date. 
[수정] Note: the US moved to T+1 settlement in May 2024, so Korea’s T+2 cycle is now longer than the current US standard.
Shorting Rules
 Short selling in Korea has been subject to periodic bans and restrictions, most recently reimposed in 2023 and partially lifted in 2025. Regulations around short selling are stricter and more politically sensitive in Korea than in Western markets.
🗓️ Trading Hours
SessionTime (KST)Pre-market auction8:00 – 9:00 AMRegular trading9:00 AM – 3:30 PMAfter-hours auction3:40 – 4:00 PM
KST = Korea Standard Time = UTC+9. No daylight saving time in Korea.
📅 Key Dates to Know
Dividend Season
 Most Korean companies pay annual dividends with a December fiscal year-end. The ex-dividend date is typically in late December, causing increased trading activity around that period.
Earnings Season
 Korean companies report quarterly, with major results typically in January (Q4/FY), April (Q1), July (Q2), and October (Q3).
